summary: Describes how Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is used over paths that span more than one IP hop, including paths where traffic may travel in only one direction on a link. It adapts the single-hop approach to longer, routed paths. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: BFD is a way for two routers to check that the path between them still works, by sending small packets at regular intervals. This RFC extends it to paths that cross several routers, where the route taken may not even be known in advance, and to links that carry traffic in one direction only.

questions: how does bfd work across multiple hops
what port does multihop bfd use
why can bfd echo not be used over multiple hops
how does bfd work on unidirectional links
subtitle: Using BFD to check paths that cross several routers, including links that carry traffic in one direction only.

tldr.problem: BFD is defined for a path between two neighbours, and three of its assumptions break when the path crosses several routers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC keeps the one-hop packet format but uses UDP port 4784, adds ways to sort the first packet of a session to the right conversation, and requires authentication because the path is now exposed to spoofing.
tldr.outcome: The Echo function is forbidden over multiple hops, and BFD multihop is for network paths rather than for application-to-application checks across the Internet.

facts.label: One-hop spoofing defence
facts.value: a TTL or Hop Limit of 255 on both transmit and receive

today: RFC 5883 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It extends the base BFD specification in RFC 5880 and the single-hop specification in RFC 5881, and it uses the UDP port that IANA assigned for BFD multihop control.

sections.title: Why BFD Over More Than One Hop
sections.content:
The Bidirectional Forwarding Detection protocol defines a method for liveness detection of arbitrary paths between systems. The BFD one-hop specification describes how to use BFD across single hops of IPv4 and IPv6.

BFD can also be useful on arbitrary paths between systems, which may span multiple network hops and follow unpredictable paths. A pair of systems may also have multiple paths between them that may overlap. This document describes methods for using BFD in such scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD is a way for two routers to check that the path between them still works, by sending small packets at regular intervals. This RFC extends it to paths that cross several routers, where the route taken may not even be known in advance.

sections.title: Where BFD Multihop Applies
sections.content:
BFD is intended as an Operations, Administration and Maintenance mechanism for connectivity check and connection verification. It is applicable for network-based services, such as router-to-router, subscriber-to-gateway, LSP and circuit endpoints, and service appliance failure detection.

In these scenarios it is required that the operator correctly provision the rates at which BFD is transmitted, to avoid congestion of a link, of input and output, or of the CPU, and to avoid false failure detection. It is not applicable for application-to-application failure detection across the Internet, because it does not have sufficient capability to do the necessary congestion detection and avoidance and therefore cannot prevent congestion collapse. Host-to-host or application-to-application deployment across the Internet will require the encapsulation of BFD within a transport that provides TCP-friendly behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD is for checking that a network path works, for example between two routers or between a customer and their gateway. It is not for checking whether a web service on the other side of the Internet is answering, because BFD cannot tell congestion apart from failure.

sections.title: Three Problems With Multihop BFD
sections.content:
There are three primary issues in the use of BFD for multihop paths.

The first is security and spoofing. The one-hop specification describes a lightweight method of avoiding spoofing by requiring a Time to Live, or Hop Limit, of 255 on both transmit and receive, but this obviously does not work across multiple hops, because every router along the path decrements it. The use of BFD authentication addresses this issue.

The second, more subtle, issue is that of demultiplexing multiple BFD sessions between the same pair of systems to the proper BFD session. In particular, the first BFD packet received for a session may carry a Your Discriminator value of zero, which leaves it ambiguous which session the packet should be associated with. Once the discriminator values have been exchanged, all further packets are demultiplexed to the proper BFD session solely by the contents of the Your Discriminator field.

The one-hop specification addresses this by requiring that multiple sessions traverse independent physical or logical links, so the first packet is demultiplexed based on the link over which it was received. In the more general case this scheme cannot work, as two paths over which BFD is running may overlap to an arbitrary degree, including the first or the last hop.

Finally, the Echo function MUST NOT be used over multiple hops. Intermediate hops would route the packets back to the sender, and connectivity through the entire path would not be possible to verify.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things break when the path is longer than one link. The trick that proves a packet came from the neighbour does not survive a router in the middle. Telling two BFD conversations apart is harder when the paths overlap. And the echo mode, where the far end sends packets back, cannot work, because the routers in between would answer first.

sections.title: Demultiplexing Packets
sections.content:
There are a number of possibilities for addressing the demultiplexing issue that may be used, depending on the application.

For totally arbitrary paths, where no part of the route is known or the known part may not be stable, a straightforward approach is to limit BFD deployment to a single session between a source and destination address pair. Multiple sessions between the same pair of systems must have at least one endpoint address distinct from one another. In this scenario the initial packet is demultiplexed to the appropriate BFD session based on the source and destination address pair when the Your Discriminator is set to zero. The approach is appropriate for general connectivity detection between systems over routed paths, and is also useful for OSPF Virtual Links.

With out-of-band discriminator signaling, the discriminator values in each direction are signalled through an out-of-band mechanism before the BFD session is established. Once learned, the discriminators are sent as usual in the BFD Control packets, so no packets with the Your Discriminator set to zero are ever sent. This method is used by the BFD MPLS specification. It is advantageous because it allows BFD to be directed by other system components that have knowledge of the paths in use, and from the point of view of a BFD implementation it is very simple. The disadvantage is that it requires at least some level of BFD-specific knowledge in parts of the system outside of BFD.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to sort the first packet of a session to the right conversation. Either each session has its own pair of addresses, or the discriminator numbers are agreed out of band before the session starts, so no packet ever arrives with a zero discriminator.

sections.title: Unidirectional Links
sections.content:
Unidirectional links are classified as multihop paths, because the return path, which should exist at some level in order to make the link useful, may be arbitrary, and the return paths for BFD sessions protecting parallel unidirectional links may overlap or even be identical. If two unidirectional links, one in each direction, are to carry a single BFD session, this can be done using the single-hop approach.

Either of the two methods above may be used in the unidirectional link case, but a more general solution can be found strictly within BFD and without addressing limitations. The approach is similar to the one-hop specification, since the unidirectional link is a single hop. The two systems are called the Unidirectional Sender and the Unidirectional Receiver. The Unidirectional Sender MUST operate in the Active role, as defined in the base BFD specification, and the Unidirectional Receiver MUST operate in the Passive role.

In the Passive role, by definition, the Unidirectional Receiver does not transmit any BFD Control packets until it learns the discriminator value in use by the other system, which happens on receipt of the first BFD Control packet. The receiver demultiplexes the first packet to the proper BFD session based on the physical or logical link over which it was received. This allows the receiver to learn the remote discriminator value, which it then echoes back to the sender in its own, arbitrarily routed, BFD Control packet, after which time all packets are demultiplexed solely by discriminator.
sections.plainLanguage: On a link that only carries traffic one way, the sending side always speaks first and the receiving side stays quiet until it has learned the other end's number. Because the link is a single hop, the receiver can sort the first packet by the link it arrived on.

sections.title: Encapsulation
sections.content:
The encapsulation of BFD Control packets for multihop application in IPv4 and IPv6 is identical to that defined in the one-hop specification, except that the UDP destination port MUST have a value of 4784. The RFC notes that this can aid in the demultiplexing and internal routing of incoming BFD packets.

Port 4784 has been assigned by IANA for use with BFD Multihop Control.
sections.plainLanguage: The packets look the same as in the single-hop case, but they go to a different UDP port, 4784, so that the router can tell multihop BFD traffic apart from other traffic on the same interface.

sections.title: Authentication and Security Considerations
sections.content:
By their nature, multihop paths expose BFD to spoofing, and as the number of hops increases the exposure to attack grows. Implementations of BFD SHOULD therefore utilize cryptographic authentication over multihop paths, to help mitigate denial-of-service attacks.

The security considerations of the RFC say the same thing again: as the number of hops increases, BFD becomes further exposed to attack, and the use of strong forms of authentication is strongly encouraged. No additional security issues are raised in this document beyond those that exist in the referenced BFD documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The longer the path, the easier it is for someone to send false BFD packets and make the link look broken. The RFC strongly recommends that BFD packets be authenticated.

items.title: Spoofing
items.text: The TTL of 255 used on a single hop does not survive a router in the middle, so authentication is needed.

items.title: Demultiplexing
items.text: The first packet of a session may carry a zero discriminator, so the session is ambiguous.

items.title: Echo function
items.text: It must not be used over multiple hops, because intermediate routers would answer instead.
